newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Costello upbeat on Australia economy, jobs scarce.
newsitem.headline: Costello upbeat on Australia economy, jobs scarce.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello gave a generally upbeat assessment of the economy in his 1997/98 (June 30) budget on Tuesday but budget documents showed little headway was expected in cutting unemployment.

"This year's budget is forecasting excellent economic prospects," Costello said when handing down the budget in parliament. "Economic growth is expected to strengthen to 3.75 percent in 1997/98, underpinned by rising private demand and favourable international developments," he said.
The government estimates that the economy will grow 3.25 percent in the year to June 1997. If the 1997/98 forecast is met, it would be the seventh year of economic expansion.
The expansion was expected to continue for at least another three years, with 3.5 percent growth projected until 2000/01.
"The stronger outlook for 1997/98 reflects stronger private consumption, the recovery in the housing sector and continued strong business investment," Costello said.

But while the pace of activity will pick up, employment will only improve moderately. Employment growth was forecast at 2.0 percent in 1997/98, up on an expected 1.25 percent in 1996/97 but below the 2.6 percent growth recorded in 1995/96.
This growth, allowing for the new job seekers it attracts to the labour force, will only be enough to cut the jobless rate to 8.0 percent by the June quarter of 1998 from 8.7 percent now.
However, if firms had more current capacity to meet increased demand than had been allowed for, the forecast employment pick up could be delayed, the budget papers said.
Inflation is expected to remain low with wages pressures moderating, Treasury forecasts in the budget papers show.
Favourable international developments would also be supportive of the economy.

Business investment is expected to ease from the strong double-digit pace of recent years. In 1997/98, business investment is forecast at eight percent, down from an estimated 16 percent in 1996/97 and 10.9 percent in 1994/95.

For its part, underlying inflation was seen near its current level, around the bottom of the Reserve Bank of Australia's two to three percent medium term target range, over 1997/98.
Also helping to keep a lid on inflation, much of the impact of the Australian dollar's rise over the past year had yet to be seen and wages growth was expected to be moderate.
Wages were forecast to grow by around four percent, allowing for impact of public sector redundancies, although Treasury warned that the risks on wages appeared evenly balanced.

Non-residential construction is expected to continue its recent rapid pace, outperforming equipment investment, driven partly by projects associated with the 2000 Olympics in Sydney and mining sector strength.
Improved housing affordability and a rundown in excess supply should help the housing sector, and growth in wages is expected to see private consumpiton accelerate, Treasury said.

The budget papers said that with consumer inflation still benefitting from cuts in interest rates it would remain under the underlying rate through 1997/98, although the gap would narrow through 1997/98. Consumer inflation is forecast at 1.75

One usual side effect of strong growth is a widening current account deficit, but Treasury said this would not be as marked in 1997/98 due to the effects of a higher dollar and commodity prices leading to an improved goods and services balance.
The deficit was forecast at A$21 billion, or four percent of GDP, in 1997/98, up slightly on 1996/97's forecast of a A$20 billion deficit, or 3.75 percent of GDP.
But not all sectors of the economy were expected to experience a better 1997/98 - the farm sector was forecast to contract by two percent.

Treasury said the fall was based on usual forecasting assumptions of average seasonal conditions following two strong years of growth which included a record wheat harvest of 23.5 million tonnes in 1996/97.
While grain production was likely to decline in 1997/98, that is expected to be offset by increased production of livestock and other crops.
